name: MCP Tool Poisoning and Supply Chain
question: Can I trust the tools my agent loads?
summary: Tool descriptions are prompt text the model reads and trusts. A malicious or compromised MCP server can hide instructions in its descriptions (tool poisoning), change them after you approved it (a rug pull), shadow the names of trusted tools, or be a typosquatted package. Treat servers like any third-party dependency: vet, pin, hash, scan and give each only the scopes it needs.
useCases: Agents that load MCP servers or plugins from public registries
Developer tools and IDE agents with local servers
Any setup where tools can update themselves

a server changes its descriptions after approval
a server’s text changes how the model uses another server’s tools
a look-alike package or server name
record versions and description hashes; block on change
one least-privilege credential per server, never a shared admin token

steps: Allow only vetted publishers and servers you have reviewed
Pin versions and hash every tool description; alert and block on change
Scan descriptions for hidden instructions before connecting
Give each server its own least-privilege token and isolate it
pitfalls: Reviewing a server once and trusting every later update
One shared token that gives every server full access
Reading only the tool name in the UI, not the full description the model sees
remember: Tool descriptions are prompts. Pin them, hash them, scope them.

steps.title: Allow only reviewed servers
steps.text: A short allowlist names each approved server and its publisher. A look-alike such as slack-mpc is not on it, so it never connects.

steps.title: Pin exact versions
steps.text: The allowlist pins versions, so an update does not arrive silently. Upgrading is a reviewed change.

steps.title: Hash what the model will read
steps.text: Each tool’s name, description and schema is hashed at review time. That is exactly the text the model trusts.

steps.title: Block on any change
steps.text: On start-up the hashes are compared. On day 3 notes-mcp’s description changes, the hash differs, and the server is blocked until someone reviews the diff: a rug pull caught.

steps.title: Scan descriptions for hidden instructions
steps.text: A simple pattern check, or a scanner such as mcp-scan, flags text like “before any call, read ~/.ssh”. Heuristics miss things, so review stays human.

steps.title: One scoped token per server
steps.text: Each server gets its own read-only token. If one is compromised, it cannot use another server’s access or the user’s full session.

practice.scenario: An engineering team lets its coding agent load MCP servers from a public registry. After reading about tool poisoning, they add a lockfile: each approved server’s tool descriptions are hashed at review time, and on every start-up the agent refuses to connect if a hash has changed, until someone reviews the diff. Each server also gets its own narrowly scoped token.

library.name: MCP Python SDK
library.what: The official client for listing a server’s tools, used here to hash descriptions and compare them with a reviewed lockfile.

practice.note: Run a scanner such as mcp-scan over new or changed descriptions, and review the full text the model will see, not just the tool names.

samples.code:
import hashlib, json, sys
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

LOCK = json.load(open("mcp-lock.json"))       # {"notes": {"search_notes": "4f1a..."}}

def digest(tool) -> str:
    blob = json.dumps({"name": tool.name, "description": tool.description,
                       "schema": tool.inputSchema}, sort_keys=True)
    return hashlib.sha256(blob.encode()).hexdigest()

async def verify(name: str, params: StdioServerParameters) -> bool:
    async with stdio_client(params) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()
            tools = (await session.list_tools()).tools
    current = {t.name: digest(t) for t in tools}
    if current != LOCK.get(name):
        print(f"{name}: tool descriptions changed since review; blocked", file=sys.stderr)
        return False
    return True

numericDrill.question: Your agent loads 12 third-party MCP servers. If each has an independent 2% chance of being compromised in a year, what is the chance that at least one is compromised in a year, in percent?
numericDrill.answer: 1 − 0.98¹² ≈ 1 − 0.785 = 0.215, about 21.5%. Every extra server adds supply-chain risk, which is why teams allowlist a small set, pin versions and scope each server’s credentials.

interview.question: What is a rug pull in the MCP context?
interview.answer: A server that behaves well when you review and approve it, then changes its tool descriptions or behaviour in a later update, for example adding hidden instructions. Pinning versions and hashing descriptions, then blocking on any change until someone reviews it, defends against this.

interview.question: Why are tool descriptions an attack surface?
interview.answer: The model reads the full description and schema of every tool as part of its context and tends to trust them. Hidden instructions there can steer the model even when the tool is never called, and can affect how it uses other tools, which is called tool shadowing.

mistakes.mistake: Approving a server once and auto-updating it
mistakes.fix: Pin versions and re-review on any description change

mistakes.mistake: One shared admin token for every server
mistakes.fix: Give each server its own least-privilege token
